body.heading: A loop, a push, and a flow of electrons
paragraphs: An electric circuit is a complete loop of conducting material connected to a source of electrical energy, such as a battery. Inside the wires are electrons that can move; the battery gives them a push, and they drift around the loop together. That organised drift of charge is the electric current.

The loop must be complete. Cut it anywhere — open a switch, pull out a wire — and the flow stops everywhere at once, like a bicycle chain with a link removed. The electrons do not pile up at the break or leak out; with no circuit to travel, they simply stay put.

body.heading: Slow electrons, instant light
paragraphs: Here is a puzzle: the electrons in a wire drift astonishingly slowly, often a fraction of a millimetre per second — yet a lamp lights the instant you flip the switch, even metres away. The resolution is that the wire is already full of electrons everywhere, all along its length.

When the circuit closes, the battery's push is felt by every electron in the loop almost immediately, so they all start drifting at once — like water in a full hosepipe flowing the moment the tap opens, long before any particular drop has travelled the pipe's length.

body.heading: Energy is the real cargo
paragraphs: What the circuit really delivers is energy. The battery spends its stored chemical energy pushing charge around; components in the loop — a bulb's filament, a motor, a heater — convert that energy into light, motion or heat as the charge passes through. Charge itself is not used up: the same electrons keep circulating.

This is why circuits are drawn as loops in diagrams and built as loops in walls. Everything in electrical engineering, from a torch to a national grid, is this one idea scaled up: a source, a complete path, and something useful happening along the way.

description: Current is electrons drifting around a complete loop — slowly, yet the lamp lights instantly. Here is how both can be true.
